connections.feedback: The Census regions are stable. They do not change every year. The disagreement comes from other sources using other definitions.
No law restricts regional naming. Other maps use different, legitimate definitions that serve other purposes.
This is partly right: people do use overlapping labels. But it describes the result more than the cause. The better answer says why the labels differ: different purposes.
connections.notes: Overlapping labels are real, but the choice describes the effect, not the reason. Marked ambiguous so the feedback can point to the better answer.

connections.feedback: Correct. A region is a human grouping. The Census Bureau groups states for statistics, while others group by landscape, history or culture.

connections.feedback: No such requirement exists for general use. Other definitions are legitimate, though a test should say which one it uses.
Correct. Statistical, cultural, economic and physical regions overlap. A good test writer names the convention being used.
This is true as a description, since overlap is common. It does not yet explain why sources differ, so it is a weaker answer than the one that points to purpose.
connections.notes: Real usage, but a description of the outcome, not its cause. Keep as ambiguous for expert level so a candidate must decide between description and explanation.

connections.feedback: Census regions have stayed fixed for long periods. Differences between maps do not come from regular regrouping.

connections.feedback: Correct. Much of the western border of the United States and Canada follows the 49th parallel north.
The Prime Meridian is a line of longitude, running north-south through Greenwich, not a latitude line.
The Mason-Dixon line is the Pennsylvania-Maryland boundary, far from the Canadian border.
The Tropic of Capricorn is far south of the equator and does not pass through North America.

connections.feedback: Correct. Mount Whitney, in California's Sierra Nevada, is the highest point in the 48 connected states.
The Cascades have tall volcanoes such as Mount Rainier, but none is as high as Mount Whitney.
The Appalachians are much lower than the western ranges. Their peaks are well below the highest western mountains.
The Rockies have many very high peaks, so this is a common guess. But Mount Whitney in the Sierra Nevada is higher than any Rocky peak.

This area is also below sea level, which makes it a good guess, but it is not as low as Death Valley.
The delta is very close to sea level and parts are slightly below it, but it is much higher than Death Valley.

connections.feedback: The Great Lakes are fresh water, not salt water. Snow forms from moisture that rises out of the lake.
Correct. This is lake-effect snow. Cold air gains heat and moisture over the lake, then releases snow when it reaches land.
In early winter the lake is usually warmer than the air. That temperature gap is what drives the snow.
Hills can add to the snow, but flat shores also get lake-effect snow. The lake's moisture is the key cause.

origin.author: READY builder

connections.feedback: Correct. Farm goods and passengers could travel by water from the interior to New York's harbor, which raised trade through the city.
The canal moved a great deal of freight, not only passengers. That freight is what boosted the port.
Ships still needed the harbor. The canal fed more goods to the port instead of replacing it.
The canal did not reach the Pacific. It connected the Hudson River with Lake Erie in the interior.
